text.p: Following are some of the leading stories in Norwegian papers this morning:

-A majority in parliament supports a proposal by Finance Minister Jens Stoltenberg to change the law on trading in shares by some investors. Managers of insurance funds must commit themselves to keeping shares they buy for personal gains at least a year under the proposal.
-A study shows that women earn between eight and 10 percent less than men with the same education and job experience.
-Norwegian authorities rebuke SAS for advertising alcohol and tobacco on SAS Trading's Internet pages in violation with Norwegian law.

-An opinion poll shows that 85 percent of Swedes think that Norwegians are good patriots, but 41 percent find them narrow-minded and only 32 percent of Swedes regard their Scandinavian neighbours as sexy.
-Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov ended a two-day visit to Oslo that Norwegian officials said was successful for the cooperation in the Arctic between the two neighbouring countries.
-Parliament will stop managers of insurance funds from trading shares for personal gains following a scandal involving a share issue in offshore group NAT.
-Kvaerner chief executive officer Erik Toenseth was dissatisfied with the 1996 results of the industrial group. He promised profits would get better this year.
